event: The ovens wake Elsie at four; it is quest day, and she is up and dressed in a rush.
She tells the plants she is off adventuring, and asks Captain to keep an eye on the others.
She packs her satchel twice, fills her water flask, and runs down past the baker's floury wave.
At the east gate in the dawn mist, Tamsin is already waiting, Margery on her back.
Cora is there too, two steps off in the mist, ledger under her arm, as if she never went to bed.
Tamsin holds up her hands, gruff: she kept Elsie's bandages clean and dry all night.
Tilly comes running, a braid freshly singed, apologising for a very small fire on Pickle Row.
Tamsin reads the notice out as the plan: two dozen open moonbells, for Mortar Lane, by morning.
Elsie, puzzled, says moonbells only open between dusk and midnight, don't they?
Tilly goes white and wails that she knew that, she said it yesterday, why didn't she say it?
Tamsin looks at the gate, the dawn, the notice, and says a word that makes the gate clerk cough.
Elsie laughs until she has to hold the gatepost; then Tilly laughs, and at last Tamsin does too.
Two steps back, Cora writes in her ledger, and the corner of her mouth moves, once.
Elsie declares that a whole free day before the work is a gift, and they should spend it together.
At a tea house on the canal, Elsie buys two pots of tea and two loaves, six pips, first.
She pours a cup for Cora herself, black, strong, one sugar, and sets it in front of her unasked.
Cora looks at the cup a long moment; then she drinks it, all of it, while it is hot.
Elsie gets out her notebook for everyone's birthdays; Tilly has to count on her fingers for hers.
Cora says her birthday is not relevant; Elsie writes, Cora: ask again.
Tilly admits she walks past Gear Street every day and can't make herself go in.
Elsie offers to go with her now, all three of them; Tilly says yes, then no, then yes.
On Gear Street the clockmaker's window ticks with a hundred clocks, and Tilly stops dead.
Through the glass her father bends over a watch, a loupe in his eye, and doesn't look up.
Tilly's hand finds Elsie's and grips it; she can't go in, and her eyes fill.
Elsie says not today, then, and that's all right; they'll come back whenever Tilly is ready.
Tamsin, gruff, puts a big hand on top of Tilly's head and steers her off down the street.
Tilly holds Elsie's hand all the way down Gear Street, and doesn't let go at the corner either.
Tamsin says they should sleep before a night's work, and nobody wants to go home alone.
They climb to Elsie's attic; the baker raises her brows at the crowd and says nothing.
Tamsin and Tilly meet Mrs Pennywhistle, Sunny, Doris and Captain; Tilly shakes Doris's leaf.
The attic has one narrow bed; Elsie says they'll all fit, and lies down in the middle.
Tamsin lies stiff on one edge; Tilly curls on the other, her nose an inch from Elsie's shoulder.
Drowsy, Elsie lays her head on Tamsin's shoulder and keeps Tilly's hand in hers.
Under her cheek Tamsin's heart pounds; Tamsin lies rigid, as if Elsie's breast on her arm burns.
Through her lashes Elsie sees Tilly staring at her mouth, until Tilly shuts her eyes hard.
Elsie thinks how lovely, friends so glad of her they can't sleep, and snuggles closer to both.
In the chair by the round window Cora is watching the three of them, and doesn't look away.
Elsie smiles at her sleepily; Cora opens the ledger and writes, and Elsie falls asleep.
In the afternoon they wake in a tangle; Tilly finds her own braid in Elsie's mouth and squeaks.
At the window, low, Tamsin asks what Elsie's class could do, if Tamsin went red tonight.
Elsie names her two skills, Captivate and Tether; she's never used either, and won't without a yes.
Tamsin says yes to Tether, now, in advance: if she goes red and turns on them, Elsie has her yes.
Elsie asks twice if she is sure; Tamsin says she has been sure since the Leftovers.
Cora, who heard every word, says flatly that the consent is noted, and writes it down.
At the booth by the east gate, a guild clerk sells them a Glasswood licence for one lantern.
Elsie pays it, since Tamsin paid for supper; Tamsin grumbles and lets her.
The clerk logs the party out and warns them: F-rank goes a mile in, to the white posts, no farther.
They walk the cart track east through the meadows for an hour as the sun goes down.
Tilly talks about moonbells the whole way; Tamsin walks close at Elsie's other side, saying little.
At dusk they reach the Glasswood, and the clear glass trees chime softly in the wind.
Glimmer moths with glass wings drift up from the grass, and Elsie gasps aloud at them.
Tamsin warns them that fallen glass cuts like a knife, so mind their hands among the roots.
In the shady hollows among the glass roots, the moonbells open blue as the light goes.
They gather on their knees side by side, counting aloud; Tilly lays each one in her apron pocket.
Kneeling, Elsie feels Tamsin watching her; when she looks up, Tamsin is looking at the moths.
A thornhare, cornered in a hollow, bites Tilly's ankle; Tilly shrieks, and Elsie binds it.
By moth-light they reach two dozen open moonbells, well short of the white posts.
Then eyes like lamps show in the trees: a pack of bramblewolves, lean and thorn-furred.
Tamsin says, very low, that nobody runs. Tilly, on her bitten ankle, turns and runs.
The wolves go for Tilly; Tamsin roars and goes red, Margery swinging, and the pack scatters.
In the Frenzy Tamsin does not stop; she wheels on the nearest shape, Tilly fallen in the roots.
Elsie throws herself between them, arms wide, and Tamsin's face has no one in it at all.
From the corner of her eye Elsie sees Cora's hand raised to Sever, held there, not used yet.
Elsie remembers Tamsin's yes, reaches for the class as she'd reach for a hand, and Tethers her.
Her window opens: Enthraller, level 1, skills Captivate and Tether, bonds Tamsin and Tilly.
Tether wakes, a warm line running both ways; Elsie knows in it that Tamsin can break it at will.
Elsie pours everything down it: Tamsin's name, Margery, the Leftovers, come back, come back.
Down the line Elsie feels the red falter, and Margery stops a foot from her face.
Tamsin's eyes clear; she sees Elsie, and Tilly behind her, and the axe's edge, and drops it.
Two wolves circle back; Tilly hurls a vial, it bursts in green fire and a bang, and the pack flees.
Tilly stares at her empty hand and says faintly that for once she meant it to explode.
Through the Tether Elsie feels Tamsin hurting: a wolf's bite on her forearm she hasn't noticed yet.
Elsie cleans and binds the bite by moth-light, then Tilly's ankle again; her hands shake only after.
Tamsin sits in the roots and sobs that nobody has ever reached her inside the red before.
Elsie holds her, Tamsin's face against her breasts, and tells her she can break the Tether any time.
Tamsin says into her that she doesn't want to break it, not ever.
Cora lowers her hand; she has severed nothing, and her pen will not stay still on the page.
Elsie asks what she wrote; Cora reads it out: Tether, with consent, to end a Frenzy. Not severed.
They limp to the empty ranger's hut at the wood's edge, the moonbells safe in Tilly's apron.
The hut has one narrow bunk; Tilly's ankle earns it, and she asks for Elsie in it with her.
Tamsin won't sleep more than a Tether's length from Elsie, so all three end up on the one bunk.
Elsie lies in the middle, Tilly's head on her breast, Tamsin at her back with an arm at her waist.
Elsie whispers goodnight, I love you both; neither answers, and she feels them both go still.
Through the Tether comes something warm and aching from Tamsin; Elsie takes it for tiredness.
Tamsin's breath is quick on her nape; Elsie thinks she must be cold, and pulls her arm tighter.
Tilly whispers, is it real, or the class? Half asleep, Elsie says it's real, she really loves them.
Tilly goes quiet, her cheek hot on Elsie's breast, and Elsie worries she has a little fever.
In the open doorway Cora sits awake against the chiming trees, keeping watch.
Cora looks back once; Elsie smiles at her, and Cora looks quickly out at the dark again.
Elsie falls asleep to the glass trees chiming, as the moonbells in the hollows close at midnight.
